Chapter 7: The Tour de France and the Meaning of Victory.
There really aren’t many events in sports as epic—or as punishing—as the Tour de France. For someone who’s stared death in the face and made it back, this race becomes more than just a competition. It’s a chance to show, not only the world but yourself, that surviving can lead to something truly extraordinary.
The months leading up to the race are intense. Every little thing counts: what you eat, the gear you choose, your strategy, and especially the fine line between pushing yourself and protecting a body that’s still healing. The team around you? They become like a second family. Each person matters, every role is crucial when you’re all chasing the same dream.
Of course, there are doubts. There are moments when the whole thing feels impossibly big—like you might get swallowed up by the pressure. But then, memories of those quiet hospital rooms, those whispered fears, come back. And suddenly, even the steepest mountain doesn’t seem so impossible.
The race itself is like a story unfolding right in front of you. Some days, you feel on top of the world—pulling off a breakaway, powering up a mountain, slipping into the yellow jersey and fighting to keep it. But there are rough days too. Crashes, flat tires, rivals just waiting to spot a weakness—every rider faces those moments. Through it all, the lessons you learned from being sick stick with you. Things like patience. Perspective. And knowing that every single mile on the bike is a victory all its own.
For the crowds lining the roads, this isn’t just about cycling. It’s about hope. It’s about proving that redemption is possible, and that the human spirit can rise above even the darkest odds. When you finally hit that finish line in Paris, it means more than just the end of a race. It’s a symbol of everything you’ve endured—and everything you’ve overcome.
And victory? It brings a storm of emotions. There’s joy, relief, gratitude, and this deep connection with everyone who’s walked alongside you, in spirit or in person. But honestly, victory isn’t the end. It brings its own set of challenges—the expectations, the public’s gaze, the pressure to keep winning. You start to realize that success, just like survival, isn’t a final destination. It’s a process. It’s waking up every day and choosing to keep moving forward, to keep believing that something better is out there—just over the next climb.
